sections.html:
Madison County's seat is Richmond, a Bluegrass city roughly 26 miles south of Lexington. Population stood at 40,663 in July 2025, compared with 35,164 in 2020, across 15,202 households. Eastern Kentucky University shapes the town: the median age is 29.1 years, and 37.4 percent of households hold a single person. Rentals and starter homes stay in demand as a result.

Renting is the norm. Under four in ten households own, so many of the houses that sell are rentals or were rentals not long ago.

The numbers below cover the five years ending 2024.

If you own a house with tenants in it, have the leases and rent records ready. Buyers will ask for them early.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or inherited house
sections.html: Landlords worn out on managing, and heirs who land a rental, can go three ways: sell while the tenants stay, hold off until the lease runs out, or find a buyer willing to step into the lease. Check the lease end date and its notice terms before replying to any offer. A cash buyer who accepts the property as is can skip the cleanout and repair cycle that usually follows a tenant move-out.

sections.h2: City permit and code rules that can slow a sale
sections.html:
Richmond's building inspection office (859-625-6428) enforces the 2018 Kentucky Building Code and related standards. A basement finished by a previous owner, a deck added on a weekend or a furnace replaced without a permit can all come to light when the buyer's inspector walks through.

  • Permits are required for new construction, structural additions, basement remodels that change the occupant load, and room additions.
  • Sheds and garages need a permit once they reach 200 square feet in a residential setting.
  • Decks and porches need one at 200 square feet, at 30 inches above the ground, or when roofed or attached to the dwelling.
  • Furnace, air conditioner and electrical panel replacements need permits, and electrical and HVAC installers who are not the homeowner need a city business license.
  • Exterior work inside the H1 historic district goes before the Architectural Review Board, and ground mounted solar is not allowed in residential sections.
  • Permit work is inspected in stages, typically footer, foundation, slab, envelope, framing or rough-in, and a final. The permit holder must call for each one.

If a seller built a deck or finished a room years ago, ask the office whether a permit was ever pulled and request a final sign-off on any open one. Applications can be filed through the city's online Accela portal or on paper at the office. Plumbing permits come from the state plumbing division or the local plumbing inspector rather than the city.

Codes Enforcement applies the property maintenance code published by the International Code Council. The board meets on the second Wednesday of each month at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall, 239 W. Main Street. Ring 859-625-6404 before listing if you think a case is open. Then you can tell a buyer where it stands, rather than letting them find it later.

sections.h2: Location and age of the house
sections.html: Interstate 75 skirts the west edge of the city, and U.S. 25 and 421 make up the eastern bypass toward Lexington. Berea lies about 14 miles south on U.S. 25. Madison County Schools covers the city. Hot, damp summers mean buyers and inspectors look hard at the age of the air conditioner.

sections.h2: Property tax bill and who pays
sections.html:
Property tax is paid to the Madison County Sheriff, 135 W Irvine, Suite B01, in person, by mail or through the online portal. Hours are weekdays, 8:00 to 4:30, and the phone is 859-623-1511. Exemptions for homestead and disability go through the county PVA at 859-623-5410. Cards work online. If your lender pays from escrow you will still get a notice, so check that the payment really went out.

Under KRS 134.015 the owner of record on the January 1 assessment date owes that year's bill. Pay by November 1 and you take 2 percent off. The face amount stands through December 31. Then a 5 percent penalty lands in January, rising to 10 percent in February. Buyer and seller usually split the year's tax at closing, but the person holding title still has to make sure the bill actually gets paid.

sections.h2: Steps for a Richmond owner who wants out fast
sections.html:
Start with the paperwork you can pull in an afternoon. Call the building inspection office and ask whether any permit on the house is still open. Call Codes Enforcement and ask the same about maintenance cases. Check with the Sheriff that the current tax bill is paid, since the debt follows whoever held title on January 1.

Next, decide how the house will be sold. A listing brings showings, an inspection and repair requests, plus a commission at closing. A cash offer on the house as it stands skips most of that, and the closing date is often your choice. Weigh the final net, not the headline number, and ask each buyer in writing what they expect you to fix, if anything.

If tenants live there, tell them early and share what the lease says about notice. Plan on handing the buyer copies of the leases and the deposit records at closing.

Timing matters too. If a tax bill is still unpaid, the sale proceeds can cover it at the closing table, but the buyer or title company will want an exact figure, so ask the Sheriff for one in advance. When a cash buyer makes an offer, ask how long they need to close, who pays the recording costs, and whether the price holds after their walkthrough. Those three answers tell you more than the offer amount does.

Finally, keep a folder of everything you collect: permit sign-offs, the tax receipt, lease copies, and any letters from the city. A tidy folder shortens the buyer's review and cuts the odds of a late surprise.

Each spring, KRS 133.045 puts the real property roll on public view for 13 days starting in early May, Saturdays included. Anyone planning to appeal has to request a conference with the PVA first.

A seller can use the conference to learn how the value was built. Bring recent neighborhood sales and ask the PVA to walk through the calculation. If the value runs higher than what nearby houses sell for, the inflated bill goes with the house to the next owner.

Kentucky's deed transfer tax falls on the seller: $0.50 for each $500 of price, with a partial block counted as a full one (KRS 142.050). The settlement statement also shows your share of the year's property tax, any mortgage or lien payoff, and a commission if an agent sold the house. A cash sale removes the commission and the repair bill, so compare what you walk away with, not the sticker price.

Before closing day, collect the payoff letter from your lender, the latest tax bill, and any permit paperwork for work done on the house. Having those in hand keeps the closing date from slipping.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed to swap out a Richmond furnace?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires a permit for furnace and air conditioner replacements and inspects the result. Call Building Inspections at 859-625-6428 before the contractor begins, since a missing permit usually shows up once a buyer's inspector looks.

faqs.q: Is Richmond mostly a renter city?
faqs.a: Largely, yes. Owners hold just 38.3 percent of households, which leaves about 62 percent renting.

faqs.q: Where does a Richmond owner send the county tax payment?
faqs.a: Send it to the Sheriff's office at 135 W Irvine, Suite B01, or pay on the sheriff's website. Do not mail cash. Weekday questions go to 859-623-1511.

faqs.q: Can a Richmond house with code violations be sold?
faqs.a: It can be, but call Codes Enforcement at 859-625-6404 first. Its board sits the second Wednesday monthly at 5:30 p.m., and you will want to know where an open case stands before a buyer asks.

faqs.q: Which transfer tax applies to a Richmond sale?
faqs.a: Kentucky charges the seller 50 cents per $500 of price, rounding a partial block up. Foreclosure deeds and some family transfers are exempt.
